# Refactor Discipline

Three classes of refactoring exist. Only two are allowed.

## A. Preparatory refactor — ALLOWED (in plan)

Before implementing a change, assess whether the existing structure will fight it. If it will, insert a preparatory refactor step into the plan *before* the implementation steps. Never skip the pre-refactor and hack the new code into a bad location.

See `dev-standards:refactor-first-assessment` for how to run the check during planning.

## B. Opportunistic refactor — FORBIDDEN

"While I'm already in this file, I may as well clean up adjacent code" is the primary source of scope creep and the primary reason plans drift. Do not do it. Touch only what the task requires.

If you notice something worth changing, record it as a review finding (see C) and move on.

## C. Review-discovered refactor — ALLOWED (as plan update)

After a task reaches GREEN, the review phase may surface C-class findings: parameter bloat, cross-task duplication, naming drift, grown responsibilities, test setup duplication, visible complexity debt, dead branches. These do NOT modify the just-finished task. They become structured **plan update proposals** that the planner decides to accept, defer, or reject.

See `dev-standards:review-for-plan-updates` for the trigger catalog, proposal format, and routing.

## Backlog configuration

Plan-update proposals carry an urgency (`low` / `medium` / `high`). `low` proposals auto-expire after 30 days to prevent unbounded backlog growth. `medium` and `high` proposals do not auto-expire. Override the expiry window by editing this file — the review skill reads it at runtime.

```yaml
backlog:
  low_urgency_expiry_days: 30
```
